ut.description: UT inspection in New York, NY: steam and process piping thickness, vessel and structural weld examination, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in New York, New York
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to buildings, utility plants, terminals and steel structures in New York for ultrasonic thickness testing and shear-wave weld examination. Typical scopes are steam and hot-water piping, pressure vessels, storage tanks, crane and bridge steel, and fabrication shop welds. Tell us the asset, the code and the access conditions through the quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in New York

New York is an infrastructure market before it is an industrial one. The steel you can see is bridges, elevated structures, crane runways and the structural frames of towers under construction. The pipe you cannot see is the dense network of steam, condensate, chilled water and fuel lines that serves hospitals, campuses, high-rise buildings and generating stations. Around the harbor there are bulk fuel storage tanks, marine terminals and the container cranes at the port complex, plus pressure vessels in power, pharmaceutical and food plants across the wider metropolitan area.

Each of those asset families asks a different ultrasonic question. A steam main in a basement vault needs wall thickness at fixed condition monitoring locations. A girder splice needs a shear-wave scan of a groove weld. A deaerator or heat exchanger shell needs thickness readings around nozzles and weld seams. UT answers all three with the same instrument family, but the procedure, the calibration blocks and the acceptance rules change with the job. You will find the general method described on our ultrasonic testing service page; this page is about how it plays out in New York.

What UT finds in New York steel and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the metal and reads the echoes. For thickness work, the time between the front-surface signal and the back-wall echo converts to remaining wall. That reading tells you how much metal is left, not why it was lost. A thinning pattern along the bottom of a horizontal steam condensate line points to a different mechanism than random pitting under wet insulation, and a technician who maps the readings in a grid sees that difference even when a single number would not show it.

For welds, an angle-beam probe puts shear waves into the joint at 45, 60 or 70 degrees. Planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks reflect sound back toward the probe and show up as indications above a reference level. Volumetric flaws such as slag reflect less strongly and need careful interpretation. UT does not tell you the material grade, cannot see through a heavily scaled or painted-over surface without preparation, and struggles with coarse cast structure and some thick stainless welds. Where those limits matter we say so before the job starts, and we point you to surface methods such as magnetic particle inspection in New York or liquid penetrant testing in New York for surface-breaking cracks that UT is not the right tool for.

Codes and jurisdictions that govern UT in New York

Which rulebook applies depends on who owns the asset. In New York City, the Department of Buildings runs a boiler unit with annual inspection and registration duties, and high-pressure boiler inspections must be done by an authorized insurance company. Outside the city, the New York State Department of Labor Boiler Safety Bureau covers boilers and unfired pressure vessels, with inspection intervals that depend on boiler type and certificates valid for 12 or 24 months. Atlantis does not replace those inspectors. We perform the examination, record the readings and hand the data to the owner's authorized inspector, who makes the call.

For the examination itself, the common references are ASME Section V, Article 4 for weld examination and Article 5 for material examination, with thickness practice following SE-797 in Article 23. Construction and repair codes decide acceptance: ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 12 for vessel welds. Structural steel on public work usually points to AWS D1.1, and state transportation department bridge steel to AWS D1.5. API 510 and API 570 govern in-service vessels and piping where the owner has adopted them, and the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for those programs. See our guide to Article 5 thickness requirements for the technique details.

How we run a thickness survey

A thickness survey starts on paper. We agree the condition monitoring locations with the owner, mark them on an isometric or a sketch, and decide how many readings make up each location. On corroded or pitted pipe we use a dual-element probe, because its split transmit and receive crystals handle rough back walls better than a single-element probe. The instrument is calibrated on a step block made of the same material as the part, with steps that bracket the expected thickness, and the A-scan is watched so that a doubled back-wall echo on thin or laminated wall is not read as a thick one.

Surface condition decides how long the job takes. Paint, scale and insulation jacketing all come off the test point first, and on older steam systems we flag insulation that may contain asbestos so that the owner arranges abatement before anyone touches it. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe, a couplant rated for the surface, and a correction for velocity change with temperature. Readings go into a grid or table keyed to the location ID so that next year's survey can be compared point for point, and any location that reads below the owner's minimum is flagged on the spot rather than at the end of the report.

Shear-wave weld examination on steel structure

Weld examination follows a written procedure. The technician sets the angle probe on a calibration block, builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes, and scans the weld from both faces where geometry allows, with the beam aimed across the fusion line. Scanning sensitivity is raised above the reference level so small indications are not lost in noise, and each reportable indication is evaluated for length, location and amplitude against the acceptance table in the governing code.

In New York that work often sits on a schedule driven by something else: a lane closure, a track outage, a crane lift window or a night shift in an occupied building. A technician who has the procedure revision, the calibration records and the weld map before arriving spends the available hours scanning instead of sorting paper. Access matters as much as technique, since a girder flange reached from a bucket lift or a swing stage gives different scan positions than the same joint in a shop. We plan probe positions and surface preparation around the access you can provide.

Who performs the work and who signs off

Technicians who perform and interpret the examinations are qualified at Level II under Atlantis NDT's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews reports before they leave; the Level III for this work is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own technicians, so the record you receive shows the technician's level, the method and the date the qualification was in force. If your own program requires a different qualification scheme, tell us at quoting time and we will say plainly whether we can meet it.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which covers how we control documents, equipment and corrective actions. It does not substitute for the owner's inspection authority, and we do not present our reports as inspector-of-record sign-off. If you need help writing or auditing the procedures your own team uses, our Level III consulting team can review them.

What a UT report from us contains

  • Asset and component identification, with the location IDs or weld numbers used in your drawings.
  • Procedure number and revision, the code edition it was written to, and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, with calibration checks recorded at start, at intervals and at the end.
  • Technician name and qualification level, and the Level III who reviewed the report.
  • For thickness: a grid or table of readings per location, nominal and minimum required thickness, and flagged low readings.
  • For welds: indication location, length, amplitude and depth, a sketch, and an accept or reject statement against the named criteria.

The point of that structure is that someone who was not on site can rebuild what happened. When a code body or an insurer's inspector asks how a reading was taken, the answer is already in the file.

Planning a UT job in New York

Several New York conditions deserve attention at quoting time. Basement vaults and mechanical rooms are often confined spaces with tight clearances, so the owner usually has to provide a permit and an attendant. Rooftop work in summer puts steel surface temperatures well above air temperature, which affects couplant choice and probe wear, and winter wind on elevated structures slows manual scanning and freezes water-based couplant, so a glycerin or gel couplant is specified. Building managers set work hours, elevators and loading docks have to be reserved, and shared sites may need certificates of insurance and safety orientations before the first technician walks in.

Because our technicians travel to your site, there is no local depot here; we say so openly and plan lodging and equipment shipment into the schedule. Atlantis has no office in New York. In return, the crew arrives with a defined scope, matching procedures and calibrated equipment rather than improvising from a general-purpose kit. For multi-day campaigns across several buildings, we will propose a sequence that keeps the readings comparable from one location to the next.

UT, MT or PT for your New York job

The three conventional methods answer different questions, and many jobs use more than one. UT measures thickness and examines weld volume. Magnetic particle inspection finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks in ferromagnetic steel and is quick on structural welds. Penetrant testing finds surface-breaking cracks in stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, where MT does not work. A bridge bearing weld might get UT for internal flaws and MT for fatigue cracks at the toe. A stainless pharmaceutical vessel would get UT thickness and PT on the weld surface. Our MT versus PT comparison helps you choose between the two surface methods, and the city pages linked above describe how we apply each in New York.

Training your own UT technicians

If you maintain an in-house inspection group, the faster route to dependable thickness data is a trained and qualified team. Atlantis teaches ultrasonic theory in UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, and technicians can practice scanning in the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator before touching real equipment. New York employers can see course options on our NDT training in New York page, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows what hours and records a candidate needs under an employer's written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have an office in New York for UT work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in New York. Level II technicians are mobilized to your building, plant or yard with calibrated equipment, a written procedure and a defined scope, and we say that plainly when we quote so travel is planned in.

faq.q: Can UT measure wall thickness through insulation or paint?
faq.a: Not through insulation. The jacketing and insulation must be removed at each test point, and paint or scale is cleaned back so the probe couples to metal. Thin tight coatings can sometimes be read with a suitable probe, but we confirm that during procedure qualification.

faq.q: Which codes do you use for ultrasonic weld examination?
faq.a: We write procedures to ASME Section V, Article 4, and apply the acceptance table of the governing construction code, such as ASME B31.3 or Section VIII, or AWS D1.1 and D1.5 for structural and bridge steel. The owner or engineer names the acceptance code before work begins.

faq.q: Who decides whether a New York boiler or pressure vessel is fit for service?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector or the jurisdictional inspector decides. In New York City that means the Department of Buildings process, and elsewhere the State Department of Labor. Atlantis performs the examination and supplies the readings and report they rely on.

faq.q: How do you handle hot steam lines during a thickness survey?
faq.a: We use a high-temperature probe and a couplant rated for the surface temperature, correct for the change in sound velocity at heat, and limit contact time on the part. Very hot lines are often surveyed during a planned shutdown instead.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a weld in New York?
faq.a: Only where the construction code, the owner and the engineer or authorized inspector allow it, and it is agreed before the job. Some codes permit UT in place of radiography under stated conditions; others do not. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States.

faq.q: What does a thickness survey report look like?
faq.a: It lists each condition monitoring location with the readings taken, nominal and minimum required thickness, any low readings flagged, instrument and calibration details, the procedure revision and the technician's qualification level, so next year's survey can be compared point for point.

faq.q: Can my staff learn ultrasonic testing through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. We offer Level 1 and Level 2 ultrasonic theory courses and a practice simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies its technicians, so the course supplies classroom hours and the employer completes experience hours, vision checks and examination records.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in New York, NY | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in New York, NY: bridge and building steel, crane welds, vessel repairs and shop fabrications. Mobilized MT crews. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in New York, New York
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to New York job sites for magnetic particle inspection of structural steel, crane and lifting equipment, pressure vessel and piping repairs, and shop fabrications. The method finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks in ferromagnetic steel and gives a result at the part while you watch. To scope a job, use the quote form; we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in New York

Most of the steel in and around New York is carbon or low-alloy steel, which is exactly what magnetic particle testing is built for. Bridges and elevated roadways carry cyclic traffic loads that open fatigue cracks at weld toes, bearing stiffeners and connection plates. Crane runway girders and the lifting gear at terminals and construction sites are inspected for cracks at pedestals, lugs and structural welds. Steel frames of high-rise towers need weld checks during erection and after any field repair. In mechanical rooms and utility plants, pressure vessel shells, support lugs, steam piping hangers and valve bodies get MT after weld repair or modification.

Fabrication shops serving the region use MT as an in-process check on fit-ups, tack welds and completed joints, when a defect is still easy to grind out. Our magnetic particle testing service page describes the method in general terms. Owners of older infrastructure often ask for MT on a sampling basis first, then widen the scope if cracking turns up; we are happy to scope it that way and to state clearly what the sample does and does not tell you. Here we cover what changes when the part is on a bridge deck, a building roof or a shop floor in New York.

What MT finds and what it cannot see

Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic material. When a magnetic field runs through a steel part and meets a crack, a small leakage field forms at the break and pulls fine iron particles into a visible line. That makes MT very sensitive to tight surface cracks that radiography and ultrasonic testing can miss. It also means austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and most nickel alloys cannot be examined this way, and for those the right method is liquid penetrant testing.

The limits are worth stating. MT finds discontinuities at or just below the surface, and sensitivity falls quickly with depth. A crack lying parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no signal, which is why ASME Section V, Article 7 calls for two examinations with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. Thick paint, weld spatter and scale reduce sensitivity, and rough surfaces create false indications that must be separated from real ones. We prepare the surface and explain what the method will and will not prove, instead of selling it as a catch-all.

Standards and acceptance for MT work in New York

The technique is set by ASME Section V, Article 7, with ASTM E709 as the guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice for the method. Acceptance does not come from the examination standard. It comes from the code that governs the asset: ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for state transportation department bridge steel. The owner or engineer names the code and edition, and we write the procedure to match.

Statutory equipment adds the jurisdiction. In New York City, boilers sit under the Department of Buildings, and high-pressure inspections must be done by an authorized insurance company. Elsewhere in the state, the Department of Labor Boiler Safety Bureau oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels. After a repair, the inspector accepts or rejects the work. Our job is to produce an MT record that makes the inspector's decision straightforward, and we ask the owner at scoping which code edition is contractually in force, since New York projects often carry older editions than the current printing. Read more about the technique in our guide to Article 7 requirements.

How the examination is performed

For field work, the usual tool is an electromagnetic yoke. Article 7 requires an alternating-current yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke to lift at least 40 pounds. We check the lifting power at the start of each shift with a certified test weight, and record it. On welds, the yoke legs straddle the joint, the technician applies particles, examines, then turns the yoke about ninety degrees and repeats so cracks in any direction can show.

Particles come in two forms. Dry powder is simple and holds up outdoors, and works well on rough weld surfaces and at moderate surface temperature. Wet particles suspended in a carrier give higher sensitivity on smooth surfaces and are normally used in shops. Fluorescent wet particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area and show fine cracks very clearly, but they need a dark enclosure that an exposed bridge deck does not provide, so a tent or a nighttime window is part of the plan. Where the code requires it, the part is demagnetized afterward so residual fields do not disturb later welding or machining.

On bare or weathered steel, a thin white contrast paint is sprayed first so that black particles stand out, and the wet-method carrier is chosen to suit the surface. Prods are avoided on finished structural members, because arcing at the contact points can leave burn marks and local hard spots that become crack starters of their own. When a part has unusual geometry, such as a pin, a thick lug or a bolted connection plate, the technician adjusts yoke position so the field passes through the area of concern, and confirms with a field indicator or a pie gauge that the field is actually strong enough where it matters.

Surface preparation and conditions on New York jobs

MT is only as good as the surface. Heavy paint, mill scale and weld slag are removed to bright metal in the examination zone, and coating thickness limits are agreed in the procedure when a thin coating stays on. Magnetic fields reach through thin nonmagnetic coatings, but sensitivity drops as thickness grows, so we qualify the technique on a sample when coating cannot be removed. On galvanized steel, the procedure addresses how zinc affects contact and particle behavior.

Weather and site conditions shape the job. On bridge steel in cold, damp weather, wet baths can freeze and oil carriers thicken, so we use dry powder or a bath concentration checked at working temperature. Wet or oily surfaces keep particles from forming indications, so they are dried and degreased. Hot surfaces such as recently welded joints must cool to the procedure limit, or a qualified high-temperature technique is used. Lighting matters too; we measure white-light intensity at the part for visible particles, and darken the area for fluorescent work.

Who performs and reviews the work

Technicians who perform and interpret MT are qualified at Level II under Atlantis NDT's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II sets up and calibrates the equipment and evaluates indications against the acceptance criteria. An ASNT Level III approves the technique sheet and reviews the report; that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own technicians, and the report shows the technician's name and level so your records are complete.

If your own team is writing MT procedures or a written practice, our written practice development service and Level III consulting can help align them to the code editions you are bound by.

What an MT report records

  • Component or weld identification, matched to the drawing or isometric you provide.
  • Procedure number and revision, the standard it was written to, and the acceptance code applied.
  • Equipment: yoke type and lifting-power check, particle type and color, carrier, and light meter reading.
  • Surface condition and temperature, and any coating left in place.
  • Technician name and level, plus the Level III who reviewed the record.
  • Indications found, with location, length and orientation, a sketch or marked photograph, and an accept or reject statement.

A crack found during a bridge inspection is only useful if someone can find it again. We mark and photograph indications and tie them to a coordinate system you can reuse during repair. On a long girder, that can be as simple as stationing from a named bearing, with each indication measured from the same datum on both the steel and the sketch, so a repair welder arriving weeks later is not guessing which toe the report meant.

Planning an MT job in New York

Practical constraints in New York affect cost and scheduling more than the technique does. Bridges and roadways often permit work only during closures, so lanes, lifts and traffic control must be coordinated with the owner. Building sites ask for safety orientation, hoisting schedules and certificates of insurance. Winter days are short, which matters for fluorescent work, and summer sun on steel can make surfaces too hot for particles. Access equipment such as bucket trucks, swing stages and scaffolding is usually the owner's or the general contractor's responsibility.

Atlantis has no office in New York, so technicians travel to your site with equipment and consumables. We plan shipping of yokes, particles and lights into the schedule, and recommend a short pre-job call to confirm access, power, lighting, and the surface-preparation plan. For multi-site programs, we propose a sequence that keeps technique and documentation consistent from one location to the next.

MT, PT or UT for your New York job

Use MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, especially structural welds and repairs. Use liquid penetrant testing in New York for stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, or when the surface is too rough or the part cannot be magnetized practically. Use ultrasonic testing in New York when the concern is internal flaws or remaining wall. Many repair packages combine them: UT to define remaining thickness around a defect, MT after the grind-out to confirm the crack is gone, and MT again on the completed repair weld. Our complete guide to magnetic particle testing goes deeper on technique choice.

Training your own MT technicians

If you want your own crew to perform magnetic particle examinations, begin with MT Level 1 training and move on to MT Level 2 training. Atlantis delivers the theory and exam preparation, and the employer completes qualification under its written practice. Employers in the area can start from our NDT training in New York page, and candidates can try questions in the NDT practice tests.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done on stainless steel in New York?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel carries no useful magnetic field, so MT cannot examine it. For stainless, aluminum and most nickel alloys we use liquid penetrant testing instead, which finds surface-breaking cracks in any non-porous material.

faq.q: Do you use a yoke or prods for field MT?
faq.a: Yokes are our default because they do not burn the surface. Under Article 7 an AC yoke must lift 10 pounds and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke 40 pounds at maximum pole spacing, and we check that at the start of each shift.

faq.q: Can MT be done in the dark on a bridge?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles need a darkened area and UV-A light, so on exposed steel we use a tent or a nighttime window. Visible dry or wet particles do not need darkness, only measured white light at the surface.

faq.q: How is a crack found on a bridge weld recorded?
faq.a: We mark the indication on the steel, photograph it with a scale, sketch its location against your reference points, and record length and orientation in the report so repair crews and later inspections can find it again.

faq.q: Does MT need paint removed?
faq.a: Heavy paint, scale and slag come off in the examination zone. A thin tight coating may stay if the procedure is qualified on a sample showing cracks still produce indications through it, and the coating thickness is recorded in the report.

faq.q: Who accepts a pressure vessel repair after MT?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector or the jurisdictional inspector accepts repairs. Atlantis performs the MT, evaluates indications against the code, and supplies the report. We do not sign off the repair on the inspector's behalf.

faq.q: Why is the magnetic field applied twice?
faq.a: A crack is detected best when it lies across the field. Applying the field in two directions at roughly right angles, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires, means cracks running in any direction cross one of the two fields.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our welders or inspectors in MT?
faq.a: We teach Level 1 and Level 2 magnetic particle theory and exam preparation. Your employer certifies its technicians under its written practice, so experience hours, vision checks and practical examinations stay with the employer, as SNT-TC-1A intends.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | New York, NY
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in New York, NY for stainless, aluminum and nickel alloy welds, castings and repairs. Mobilized PT technicians. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in New York, New York
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to sites in New York for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, of welds, castings, machined parts and repair excavations. PT is the method of choice for stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, where magnetic particle testing cannot work. Describe the material, surface and code in the quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in New York

New York buildings and plants contain a surprising amount of nonmagnetic metal. Hospitals, laboratories and pharmaceutical facilities run stainless steel piping and vessels for clean steam, water for injection and process fluids. Food and beverage plants in the region use stainless tanks and sanitary lines. Ferries and harbor craft use aluminum structure and fittings, and propeller and shaft components in the working harbor are often bronze or stainless. Power and utility plants have stainless welds in feedwater and chemical systems and nickel-alloy components in high-temperature service.

PT also shows up on carbon steel when MT is impractical, such as inside a narrow nozzle, on a thin-walled component or after a repair where the surface condition is mostly what matters. Our general penetrant testing page describes the method; this page explains how we apply it on New York work, from vaults and roof plants to shop floors.

What PT finds and what it cannot find

Penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid is applied, seeps into any crack or pore, and after excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped liquid back out where it shows as a bleed-out line or dot. Because the test relies on capillary action, it works on almost any non-porous material, including steel, stainless, aluminum, titanium and many nonmetals, and it excels at fatigue cracks, grinding cracks, shrinkage cracks and lack of fusion that reaches the surface.

The weaknesses are equally clear. A flaw that does not break the surface will not show, and a crack smeared closed by blasting, machining or peening can hide completely. Porous surfaces and rough castings soak up penetrant and give false indications. Dirt, oil, paint or rust block entry and cause missed cracks. Because of that, cleaning is the most important step, and mechanical cleaning that smears metal over a crack, such as wire brushing or shot blasting, is usually avoided before PT. Penetrant sensitivity also varies by system. A fluorescent penetrant used with a dry-powder developer reveals finer cracks than a visible-dye system, but it demands a darkened area and a trained eye, so the choice is a trade between sensitivity and practicality that the procedure states in advance. On tight fatigue cracks in a stainless vessel, for example, the longer dwell and the fluorescent method are often justified, while a general weld surface check on a steam line may be satisfied with visible dye. If your concern is below the surface, ultrasonic testing in New York is the better choice.

Codes and acceptance for PT in New York

The technique comes from ASME Section V, Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the practice for general industry. Acceptance criteria come from the code that governs the asset: ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.5 where PT is permitted on structural or bridge welds. Article 6 also limits sulfur in penetrant materials used on nickel alloys and halogens in materials used on austenitic stainless steel and titanium, so the product lot matters on those materials.

Pressure equipment adds a jurisdiction. In New York City the Department of Buildings oversees boilers, and elsewhere in the state the Department of Labor Boiler Safety Bureau covers boilers and unfired pressure vessels. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, and the inspector, not the NDT contractor, accepts the repair. Our task is to deliver a PT record that names the materials, times and temperatures clearly enough for that decision. See our guide to Article 6 requirements for the detail.

How a penetrant examination is carried out

The sequence is: clean, apply penetrant, dwell, remove excess, apply developer, examine, record, clean up. Each stage has a control that the technician checks, from the cleanliness of the surface to the condition of the developer coat, and a missing control invalidates the result. Penetrants are classified by type, with fluorescent materials examined under UV-A light and visible dye materials examined in white light, and by method, which describes how excess is removed: with water, with an emulsifier, or with solvent. For most field welds and repair excavations in New York, a visible-dye, solvent-removable system is the practical choice because it needs no water supply or power. Fluorescent systems give more sensitivity and are used where the code or the part calls for it, with a darkened area and a meter reading of the UV-A intensity at the surface.

Dwell time is set by the procedure and the material, and the developer has a time window in which interpretation must happen. We time each step and record it. Excess penetrant is removed by wiping with lint-free material, first dry and then lightly dampened with solvent, never by flooding the surface, because over-removal washes penetrant out of a real crack. After examination the part is cleaned so that residues do not interfere with welding, coating or product contact.

Temperature and surface conditions in New York

ASME Section V, Article 6 sets a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit (about 5 to 52 degrees Celsius) for both the part and the penetrant materials. Beyond those limits, the procedure has to be demonstrated at the temperature actually encountered. New York gives both extremes. In winter, outdoor piping and structure on a rooftop or at the waterfront are well under 40 degrees and penetrant becomes thick and slow to enter fine cracks. In July, dark steel in direct sun can exceed 125 degrees, and penetrant dries on the surface before dwell is finished.

We handle that by planning. Humidity and rain matter as well, because water in a crack blocks the penetrant, so we dry the surface and shelter the work area. Cold jobs use a heated enclosure, a warm-up of the part, or a non-standard temperature technique qualified on a comparator block. Hot jobs are shifted to cooler hours, shaded, or the part is cooled before application. Surface temperature is measured and entered in the report along with the times.

Who does the work and who reviews it

Level II technicians qualified under Atlantis NDT's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A, perform and interpret the examinations. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report, and that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A each employer certifies its own personnel, so your file shows who performed the work, at what level, and under which procedure revision.

Because PT results can depend on small details such as lot numbers and dwell times, the Level III checks that the report documents them. A periodic system performance check on a known cracked panel, also called a comparator, shows whether the materials in use still reveal fine cracks, and that check is recorded alongside the job. If your own procedure for PT needs a rewrite to match a code edition, our Level III consulting and written practice development services can help.

What the PT report contains

  • Component or weld identification, matched to your drawing or isometric.
  • Procedure number and revision, standard and acceptance code, with the penetrant type and method.
  • Materials: manufacturer, product names and lot numbers for cleaner, penetrant and developer, with contaminant certifications when the base metal requires them.
  • Surface preparation, surface temperature, dwell time, developer time and examination conditions.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III who reviewed the record.
  • Indications with location, size and type, a photograph or sketch, and an accept or reject statement.

Where an owner keeps an indication log across several inspection cycles, we number indications so the same weld toe can be compared over years. Photographs with a scale are included whenever the site permits, because a bleed-out pattern fades as the developer dries and the photograph is the lasting record.

Planning a PT job in New York

Penetrant materials are flammable solvents, so work in occupied buildings, mechanical rooms and confined spaces needs a hot-work and ventilation plan agreed with the owner before we arrive. Cleaning solvents and developer must be approved for the site and any chemical restrictions on stainless or nickel alloy systems checked. Waste cloths and aerosol cans are removed by the technicians. Scheduling also deserves attention: PT is slow compared with MT because of dwell and cleaning, so jobs involving many welds are planned in batches. A realistic plan separates cleaning, application, dwell and examination into stages that run in parallel across several welds, so one technician is always examining while the next set of joints is still dwelling. Owners who want to compress a shutdown should raise this at quoting time, because adding a second technician is usually more effective than shortening dwell, which the procedure does not allow.

Atlantis has no office in New York. Technicians travel to your site with consumables from controlled lots, which matters because penetrant products are matched to the procedure. We suggest a pre-job call to confirm materials, access, temperature expectations and whether the owner supplies water, power and lighting for fluorescent work.

PT, MT or UT for your New York job

PT is the right choice for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, bronze and any part that cannot be magnetized, and for surface checks in tight geometry. For carbon steel structure and welds, magnetic particle inspection in New York is often faster and finds slightly subsurface cracks as well. Wall loss and weld volume call for ultrasonic testing. A common pharmaceutical vessel package uses UT for shell thickness and PT on welds and repairs, and the MT versus PT comparison gives a decision table.

Training your own PT technicians

Penetrant testing is one of the quickest methods to learn and a common starting point for new technicians. Atlantis teaches the theory in PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and learners can rehearse in the penetrant testing simulator. See the local options on our NDT training in New York page.

faq.q: What is the difference between dye penetrant and liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: They are the same method. Dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing both describe PT, where a liquid enters surface-breaking cracks and a developer draws it back out. Visible-dye and fluorescent versions exist.

faq.q: Can PT be done outdoors in a New York winter?
faq.a: Yes, with planning. The standard range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Below that we use a heated enclosure or a procedure qualified at the lower temperature, and we record the surface temperature in the report.

faq.q: Does penetrant testing find internal flaws?
faq.a: No. PT finds only discontinuities open to the surface. For internal flaws or remaining wall we use ultrasonic testing, and often combine the two on the same vessel or weld.

faq.q: Is PT safe to use on stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes, when the materials are controlled. ASME Section V Article 6 limits halogens for use on austenitic stainless steel and titanium, and sulfur on nickel alloys, so we use lots with documented contaminant content and record them.

faq.q: Why is the surface cleaned so carefully before PT?
faq.a: Oil, paint, rust and smeared metal can block a crack so the penetrant never enters. Careful cleaning, usually with solvents and lint-free cloths and without wire brushing or blasting, is the most important step in a reliable penetrant test.

faq.q: How do you record a penetrant indication?
faq.a: We photograph it with a scale before the developer dries, sketch its position against your reference points, and log size, type and location in the report with the times and temperature, so later inspectors can compare.

faq.q: Do you need power and water on site for PT?
faq.a: Solvent-removable visible-dye systems need neither. Fluorescent work needs power for a UV-A lamp and a darkened area. We agree what the site provides before mobilizing so the right system is brought.

faq.q: Can my team be trained in penetrant testing through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. We run Level 1 and Level 2 penetrant theory courses and a simulator for practice. Your employer certifies technicians under its written practice, completing experience hours, vision checks and practical examinations as SNT-TC-1A requires.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in New York, NY: What We Do Instead
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For New York, NY we can discuss UT as a volumetric option, Level III image review and RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in New York, New York
rt.html:
If you searched for radiographic testing in New York, here is the plain answer: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity. It is regulated under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules, 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State such as New York, and it is not a service Atlantis offers here. We would rather tell you now than waste your week.

The alternatives below suit many people who start with an RT search: ultrasonic examination as a volumetric option where the code allows it, independent Level III review of radiographs made by someone else, and radiography theory training.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative in New York

Radiography is chosen because it looks through the full thickness of a weld. Ultrasonic testing does the same job by a different physical route, with shear-wave probes scanning the weld volume and no radiation exclusion zone. In a dense city that matters: radiographic work in occupied buildings, on streets or beside transit is restricted because of exposure to the public, while ultrasonic work needs only access and a clean surface.

Substitution is not automatic. The process piping code ASME B31.3 and the pipeline code API 1104 each contain ultrasonic provisions for production welds, AWS D1.1 carries separate acceptance criteria for groove welds examined ultrasonically, and ASME Section VIII lets UT stand in for radiography only when specific conditions are met. Any change of method must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job. Our ultrasonic testing in New York page describes the scope, and you can send details through the quote form.

Level III review of radiographs and RT procedures

Many New York projects, from piping fabrication to building mechanical work, receive radiographs made by a licensed contractor and then need someone to read them with an independent eye. A Level III holding ASNT certification reads the film or digital images, the technique sheet and the exposure records against ASME Section V, Article 2 and the construction code, then writes up what the images do and do not show. This needs no radiation licence, because the reviewer handles images and paperwork and never a source.

The same review covers a second read of disputed indications, and an audit of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts. Our reviewer is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, which is why he can read the images competently without ever handling a source. See NDT Level III consulting for how these engagements are scoped, and our written practice development page if your own RT program needs documents.

What to send for an RT alternative in New York

To scope either option quickly, send the drawing or isometric, the weld list with material and thickness, the construction code and edition, the acceptance criteria the owner has named, and any contract wording that calls for radiography. If the radiographs already exist, send a few sample images and the technique sheet so the reviewer can say what a full review would involve. Also mention how the work is scheduled: ultrasonic work in a building can be planned around occupied hours, which radiographic work often cannot.

Radiography training and surface methods

For those building their own program, the theory side of radiography is taught in our radiographic testing Level 2 course. Radiation safety training and licensing remain with the regulator and the licensed employer, and the course covers the NDT theory and not the licence. Employers in the metro area can also start from NDT training in New York.

When the concern is surface cracking rather than internal flaws, magnetic particle inspection in New York and liquid penetrant testing in New York cover steel and nonmagnetic metals. Atlantis technicians are mobilized to your site for those methods, and we have no office in New York. Our state page for inspection services in New York lists the full set of conventional services.

faq.q: Can Atlantis NDT do radiography in New York?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is a licensed activity under NRC rules or Agreement State rules and is not a service we offer. We offer ultrasonic testing, image review and training instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code, the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector agree before the job. Some codes allow ultrasonic examination of production welds under stated conditions, and others require radiography. We help you read the code position.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs made by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III can go through film or digital images and technique sheets with ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code in hand, give a second opinion on disputed indications, and audit the contractor's own procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Do I need a licence for Atlantis to review radiographs?
faq.a: No. Reviewing images and records involves no radiation source, so no radiation licence applies to the reviewer. The licensed contractor who made the exposures remains responsible for the radiography and its safety.

faq.q: Can I learn radiography theory through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Radiographic theory is covered in our Level 2 course. That course leaves out radiation safety licensing, which stays with your regulator and licensed employer, and certification of technicians remains with the employer under its written practice.
